descriptor: Retail franchisor & property owner · Jun FY · reported in AUD

charts.title: Gross Profit, Operating Income & Net Income

sections.title: Franchise Model & Property Investment
sections.subtitle: Harvey Norman splits revenue between direct sales and franchise fees, and capex between ordinary assets and freehold property

charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

revenueSplit.title: Sales revenue vs franchise revenue
revenueSplit.content:
Sales revenue is turnover from company-operated (complex) stores; franchise revenue is the fees, service charges and property income Harvey Norman earns from its network of independently owned franchisees.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: the franchise model is central to the business -- franchisees fund their own inventory and working capital, and franchise revenue is a structurally higher-margin, lower-capital-intensity line than direct sales. The split shows how much of group growth is coming from the franchisor economics versus the company's own retail operations.

What to watch:

  • Franchise revenue growing faster or slower than sales revenue
  • Franchise revenue as a share of the total -- a rising share implies a lighter-capital mix
  • Interim swings that mirror store network changes (conversions between franchised and company-operated)

capexSplit.title: CapEx: PP&E vs investment property
capexSplit.content:
PP&E & intangibles capex is ordinary reinvestment in fixtures, IT and store fit-out. Investment property capex is cash spent acquiring or developing freehold property that Harvey Norman then lets to franchisees and external tenants.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: the group owns roughly A$4.8bn of freehold property, and buying rather than leasing store sites is a deliberate part of the strategy -- it captures the rental economics a pure retailer would pay away, but it also means capex is only partly a growth-in-retail-operations signal; a chunk of it is property investment with its own return profile.

What to watch:

  • Investment property capex spiking around site acquisitions, distinct from steady-state PP&E reinvestment
  • Total capex relative to operating cash flow (see Operating Cash Flow & CapEx below)
  • Whether property capex is funded from operating cash or debt

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Harvey Norman Holdings Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
